claims.text: The proposed multi-step thermo-mechanical route will produce a uniform nanoscale distribution of coherent precipitates and controlled deformation twins in high-entropy alloys.
The combined precipitates and deformation twins will synergistically enhance strength, ductility, Young’s modulus, and fracture resistance.
Conventionally arc-melted and annealed high-entropy alloys exhibit a coarse, less-refined microstructure typical of state-of-the-art processing.
Rapid solidification will refine the alloy's grain structure.
Aging at approximately 500°C for one hour will form a uniform distribution of nanoscale precipitates.
Room-temperature thermo-mechanical rolling or tensile pre-straining at a moderate strain rate will induce deformation twins.
The precipitates formed by the process will be coherent.
Nanoscale precipitates obstruct dislocation motion and thereby increase strength through dispersion strengthening.
Deformation twins accommodate strain and thereby enhance ductility.
The refined precipitate-and-twin microstructure increases effective Young’s modulus.
The refined precipitate-and-twin microstructure improves fracture resistance by increasing energy absorption during deformation.
The proposed route will increase yield strength by approximately 15–20% relative to conventional annealing.
The proposed route will increase ductility by approximately 10–15% relative to conventional annealing.
The proposed route will increase fracture toughness by approximately 10–15% relative to conventional annealing.
The proposed route will produce a modest increase in Young’s modulus relative to conventional annealing.
The approach is expected to work primarily in compositional ranges that support stable multi-principal-element solid-solution phases.
Substantial deviations in composition or processing parameters can cause secondary-phase instability or coarse precipitates that negate the proposed property synergy.

contradictions.description: The central hypothesis predicts enhancement of all four target properties, but the stated rule treats improvement of only two properties by at least 10% as sufficient to avoid falsification, even if the other two fail to improve or deteriorate.
